Supreme Court of Newfoundland — Court of AppealR. v. SimpsonDate: 19940316Docket: 1993no.210 GOODRIDGE C.J.N.:— The issues in this case are:(1) whether the police violated s. 503(l) of
the Criminal Code by failing to bring the respondent, a person charged
with an offence punishable by imprisonment for more than five years, before a
justice within the time limits prescribed in that subsection(2) whether such violation constituted a
violation of the respon­dent's right under s. 9 of the Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms not to be arbitrarily detained, and (3) if there was such a violation of s.
503(1) and if such violation constituted a breach of the s. 9 Charter right,
whether a judicial stay of proceedings under s. 24(1) of the Charter was an appropriate and just remedy.The chargeThe respondent was charged with assault causing
bodily harm and public mischief. The information against her contains the
following counts:Count No. 1On or about the 8th day of August, A.D.,
1992, at or near St. John's, in the province of Newfoundland, did unlawfully
commit an assault that caused bodily harm to Teresa Bolt, thereby committing an
indictable offence, contrary to Section 267(1)(b) of the Criminal Code of
Canada.

Count No. 2On or about the 8th day of AUGUST, A.D., 1992,
at or near St. John's, in the Province of Newfoundland, did commit public
mischief in that with intent to mislead a Peace Officer of the Royal
Newfoundland Constabulary to enter upon or continue an investigation by making
a false statement that accused Garry Allen of having committed an offence under
Section 267(1)(b) of the Criminal Code of Canada (ASSAULT CAUSING BODILY HARM), thereby committing an indictable offence, contrary to section 140(î)(a)-140(2)(a)
of the Criminal Code of Canada.The factsThe respondent was arrested in relation to the
charges on Sunday, March 14, 1993, at 1:30 p.m. She was detained by the police
until brought before a judge of the Provincial Court on Tuesday, March 16,
1993, when she was released on an under-taking. This was just under 48 hours
from the time of her arrest.Monday, March 15, 1993, was a provincial
holiday.The respondent's appearance before a Provincial
Court judge on Tuesday, March 16, 1993, was her first appearance before a
justice after her arrest on Sunday, March 14, 1993. The information against her
was also sworn on March 16, 1993, two days after her arrest.On August 16, 1993, the respondent, alleging
that the police had failed to comply with s. 503 of the Criminal Code and
had thereby violated her s. 9 Charter rights, applied for a remedy pursuant to
s. 24(1) of the Charter. The remedy which she sought was a judicial stay of
proceedings; she did not request any other remedy. On October 18, 1993, Kennedy
Prov. Ct. J. granted the requested stay. The trial judge concluded that the
police had failed to comply with s. 503 of the Code, that this failure
constituted a breach of s. 9 of the Charter and that the only appropriate and
just remedy was a judicial stay as, in his opinion, it was not appropriate to
permit the charges to proceed.

A person described in s-s. (1) is a person who
has been arrested with or without a warrant. Neither of the charges against the
respondent is included in the offences mentioned in s. 522.Section 503(2) is not absolutely clear. It
provides that a peace officer who is satisfied that an arrested person may be
released from custody conditionally may release that person in
accordance with s. 498(l)(f) to (h). These paras. (f) to (h) prescribe
no conditions except a promise to appear.As will appear, the police officer in this case
wanted to release the respondent conditionally. The condition was that the
respon­dent would stay away from certain persons. He saw no way of imposing
such condition and therefore held the respondent until she could appear before
a justice of the peace (in this case, a Provincial Court judge) who was
empowered under s. 515 of the Criminal Code to impose conditions if
Crown counsel established that such conditions should be ordered.Putting all this together, it means that a
person such as the respondent who has not been released under s. 503(2) of the Criminal
Code shall be brought before a justice without unreasonable delay and in
any event within 24 hours. When a justice is not available, the arrested person
shall be brought before a justice as soon as possible.

Sections 9 and 24(1) of the Charter provide:9. Everyone has the right not to be
arbitrarily detained or imprisoned.24(1) Anyone whose rights or freedoms, as
guaranteed by this Charter, have been infringed or denied may apply to a court
of competent jurisdiction to obtain such remedy as the court considers
appropriate and just in the circumstances.The hearingThere was a pre-trial application for a stay of
proceedings, a remedy sought under s. 24(l) of the Charter on the basis that
the s. 9 Charter right of the respondent had been denied by virtue of the
failure of the police to bring the respondent before a justice without
unreasonable delay.Sergeant Roger Tinkam of the R.C.M.P testified
that, in non-urban areas of Newfoundland, the R.C.M.P have an arrangement with
justices of the peace to bring arrested persons before them pursuant to s. 503
as required. The need for such an arrangement is more demanding in the
non-urban areas where a Provincial Court judge would not be regularly in
attendance from Monday to Friday. Without having such an arrangement with
justices of the peace, an arrested person might have to remain in custody for
several days before being brought before a justice.However, Sergeant Tinkam pointed out that in
areas patrolled by the R.C.M.P. which are near St. John's, it is not uncommon
for a person arrested on a weekend not to be brought before a justice until
Monday morning when the Provincial Court opens.

Constable G.E. Crocker of the Royal Newfoundland
Constabu­lary was the arresting officer. He advised that he was contacted by
the complainant on February 28, 1993, about the charges against the respondent.
This could not have been the first time that the subject matter of the
complaints had come to the attention of the police as count 2 alleges that the
respondent made a false statement to the police on August 8, 1992. No
explanation was given as to what, if anything, transpired between August 8,
1992, and February 28, 1993, but evidently something was said to Constable
Crocker on February 28, 1993, that led him to the conclusion that the arrest of
the respondent was desirable.Nothing transpired for two weeks. Constable
Crocker himself was away for a portion of that period and, apparently, no other
police officer was assigned to the case. Constable Crocker indicated that he
made two calls at the home of the respondent and received no response. He did
find her there on Sunday, March 14, 1993, at which time he arrested her.The arrest was, apparently, based on Constable
Crocker's belief that the respondent had committed an indictable offence. The
information had not been sworn out at that time.There were other procedures that might have been
employed by Constable Crocker in accordance with the Criminal Code, such
as a summons which could have been issued by a justice following the laying of an
information.

Constable Crocker, however, felt that the
respondent should be detained and released only upon the condition that she
remain away from and not communicate with certain identified persons.Sergeant J.H. Baggs of the Royal Newfoundland
Constabulary, the respondent herself and Deputy Chief Leonard Power of the
Royal Newfoundland Constabulary also testified. The evidence of the respondent
herself did not really assist in the determination of the issue.Sergeant Baggs and Deputy Chief Power spoke of
the practice of the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary with respect to week-end
arrests. They mentioned a manual of instructions provided to the police
officers and presumably prepared by the constabulary or, for its benefit, by
the department of justice.This manual does not apparently contain any
direction with respect to persons who are arrested on a week-end and whom the
police are either unwilling or unable to release. If not released, such persons
are simply held in custody until they can be brought before a Provincial Court
judge on Monday morning or, if Monday is a holiday, on Tuesday morning.In Corner Brook, the constabulary does bring
weekend arrests before a justice without waiting for Monday morning to arrive.The judgmentThe judgment of the Provincial Court was given
by Kennedy Prov. Ct. J. He gave careful thought to the issues that had been
presented to him. He noted that the Provincial Court judges sit on a regular basis
from Monday to Friday in St. John's and are available on the week-ends for
limited purposes, such as dealing with requests for autopsy orders and for
search warrants. These are matters that generally do not require a formal
hearing and can be dealt with from the home of the judge.

trained to deal with hearings for judicial interim release.He held that the failure of the police to bring
the respondent before a justice within the times limited by s. 503 was a
violation of that section which resulted in an arbitrary detention of the
respondent. He went on to hold that a stay of proceedings was the only remedy
available and he so ordered.Section 503(1)This section requires the arresting officer to
bring an arrested person, who is not released under any other provision of the Criminal
Code, before a justice without unreasonable delay to be dealt with
according to law. It is sometimes thought that the police may detain such a
person for 24 hours. The dominant time factor is "without unreasonable
delay" and the limit placed on this period is 24 hours. An unreasonable
delay could nevertheless occur in less than 24 hours. It should not be assumed therefore
that a violation of s. 503(1) is not taking place notwithstanding that
24 hours has not expired.Section 503(l)(b) provides that, where a
justice is not available within 24 hours after the person has been arrested,
the person shall be taken before a justice as soon as possible. It seems that
this is being relied upon by the police to justify the continuation of
detention on a week-end until the Provincial Court opens on Monday morning.
While the purpose of this enactment is not absolutely clear, it probably
applies to situations where a person is arrested in a remote area where a
justice is not available. It cannot be said to apply to an arrest in the City
of St. John's where there are a large number of Provincial Court judges and 55
justices of the peace. It is ludicrous to say in those circumstances that a
justice is not available within a 24-hour period. It is difficult to conceive
of any circumstances in St. John's (and probably in most parts of Newfoundland
although this judgment only puts in issue police practices in St. John's) where
the police could rely on s. 503(1)(b) to justify detaining an arrested person
until the Provincial Court opened on Monday morning or Tuesday morning as the
case might be.

input:
Section 503 may be one of the most
important procedural provisions of the Criminal Code. The liberty of the
subject is dominant. A person not convicted of an offence should never be held
in custody except in accordance with constitutionally valid provisions of the Criminal
Code or other legislation. In some jurisdictions, even during the sitting
week, the police will bring an arrested person before a justice, as soon as the
various tasks that generally follow an arrest are completed, for hearing as to
whether the person should be released or detained. If necessary, a trial will
be interrupted for this purpose.The paramountcy of the liberty of the subject
has been recog­nized in English law from the earliest times. Freedom is a
fundamental right. It is not to be taken away except in strict accordance with
the law.The prerogative writ of habeas corpus was
developed as a remedy for unlawful detention. The superior courts are entrusted
with the function of ensuring that any person improperly detained shall be
released.Where a person is arrested with or without a
warrant, it is the duty of the arresting officer to ensure that that person is
not detained any longer than is absolutely necessary and that, if he or she is
not authorized by law to bring about the release, the person is brought before
a justice of the peace who may determine whether the detention should continue
or not and, if it is not to continue, what lawful conditions should be attached
to the release.

input:
The peace officer, of course, has a problem. In
this case Constable Crocker was required to bring the respondent before a
justice without unreasonable delay. The particular delay in this case appears
to have been about 90 minutes which would have brought the time to about
mid-afternoon on Sunday. How was he to go about finding a justice of the peace
ready, willing and able to preside at a hearing at that time?There was a practical problem. The Provincial
Court judges did not, at that time, sit on week-ends. There were duty judges
but their function as duty judges was, apparently, to deal with ex parte process.
There were 55 justices of the peace other than Provincial Court judges in the
city area. The constabulary does not appear to have been particularly aware of
this fact and, in any event, there is no indication that any of the justices
were trained in the judicial process with respect to hearings for judicial
interim release.There was no indication before the court as to
what the practice in this respect in other provinces is. The problem in St.
John's is currently being taken care of by Provincial Court judges who hold
hearings in the court-house near the lock-up on Saturday and Sunday mornings.That there is a practical problem is clear. It
is not, however, for the Court of Appeal to determine what the solution to the
problem is. All the court can say is that if s. 503 is to be complied with
(and, of course, there must be compliance), there must be justices as defined
available before whom people arrested on week-ends who cannot be released
except by order of a justice may be brought without unreasonable delay. What
has happened in this case should never be allowed to happen again.

input:
Charter, s. 9Crown counsel argued before this court that the
detention in this case was not an arbitrary detention. The discussion revolved
around the meaning of the word "arbitrary". There is a tendency to
resort to dictionary definitions. This resort generally leads to other words
which themselves need defining. Constable Crocker himself had probably given no
thought as to whether his decision to hold the respondent until conditions
could be placed upon her release was arbitrary. If he had been fully aware of
and understood the provisions of s. 503(1) and knew the responsibilities which
lay upon him as set forth above, and nevertheless decided to hold the respondent
until she could appear in the Provincial Court on Tuesday morning, there would
be little doubt that the detention was arbitrary.This raises the question as to whether it is any
less arbitrary because Constable Crocker appears not to have been fully aware
of his legal obligations in this respect. To take this position is to define
arbitrary from a subjective point of view, from the point of view of the detainer
and not the detainee.It is true, of course, that the respondent, when
brought before a justice, might not have been released. She was in fact never
given the opportunity to seek her own release (except technically by habeas
corpus which was not a practical alternative in the circumstances of this
case). If she had been given that opportunity and was denied her freedom, her
detention would then have been lawful. Unless and until judicial interim
release was denied, however, once the period that is denoted by the words
"without unreasonable delay" had expired and until she was thereafter
brought before a justice there was certainly an unlawful detention.

input:
Counsel argued and it is acknowledged that an
unlawful deten­tion is not necessarily an arbitrary detention. An unlawful
deten­tion may result from a technical error of process. Here there was a major
violation of a statutory provision protecting the fundamental right of the
respondent to be free unless properly detained by law. It is an understatement
to describe such detention as unlawful. It must be viewed as arbitrary. There
was a failure of a policeman to carry out his duty under the law which, whether
deliberate or simply neglectful, resulted in the respondent being detained. By
act or neglect, the administrative or judicial system, or both, failed the
respondent. A neglect to follow s. 503(1) or to provide the mechanism by which
s. 503(1) may be followed is just as arbitrary as a positive decision not to
follow s. 503(l).The respondent must be considered to have been
arbitrarily detained and to be entitled to apply for a remedy under s. 24(1) of
the Charter.Charter, s. 24(1)Section 24(1) of the Charter provides that
anyone whose rights or freedoms have been infringed or denied may apply to a
court of competent jurisdiction to apply such remedy as the court considers
appropriate and just in the circumstances.The question arises as to what is a court of
competent jurisdic­tion. This is a question that involves many considerations.
It is not proposed to examine the question in its broadest context but rather
to consider it within the confines of a case such as the one before court. The
decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in R. v. Mills (1986), 26 C.C.C.
(3d) 481, 29 D.L.R. (4th) 161, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 863 (S.C.C.), although given by
a divided court, has offered some light on the issue of what is a court of
competent jurisdiction. The court was in agreement that a judge presiding at a
preliminary inquiry is not a court of competent jurisdiction for the purpose of
granting a remedy under s. 24(l). The court before whom an accused person is
being tried is a court of competent jurisdiction.

For the purposes of this case, there is no
dispute as to the right of the trial judge to consider a s. 24(1) application.
For reasons already stated there should likewise be no dispute that the
respondent was entitled to obtain such remedy as the trial judge considered
"appropriate and just in the circumstances". In Mills, McIntyre
J. said at p. 493:These courts will be courts of competent
jurisdiction, where they have jurisdiction conferred by statute over the offences
and persons and power to make the orders sought. It is to be hoped that trial
judges will devise, as the circumstances arise, imaginative remedies to serve
the needs of individual cases. Such remedies must remain, however, subject to
constitutional restraint, that is, they must remain within the ambit of
criminal powers. A claim for a remedy under s. 24(1) arising in the course of
the trial will fall within the jurisdiction of these courts as a necessary
incident of the trial process.He continued at pp. 501:What remedies are available when an
application under s. 24(1) of the Charter succeeds? Section 24(1) again is
silent on the question. It merely provides that the appellant may obtain such
remedy as the court considers "appropriate and just in the
circumstances". It is difficult to imagine language which could give the
court a wider and less fettered discretion. It is impossible to reduce this
wide discretion to some sort of binding formula for general application in all
cases, and it is not for appellate courts to pre-empt or cut down this wide
discretion. No court may say, for example, that a stay of proceedings will
always be appropriate in a given type of case. Although there will be cases
where a trial judge may well conclude that a stay would be the appropriate
remedy, the circumstances will be infinitely variable from case to case and the
remedy will vary with the circumstances.

Mills makes it
clear that a criminal trial court is a court of competent jurisdiction to grant
s. 24(1) remedies while the matter in which the question of a Charter violation
rises is sub judice. What is less clear, however, is what type of
remedies may be given. McIntyre J., in Mills, suggested that the remedy
must be within the ambit of the criminal powers of the trial court. This would
seem to exclude civil remedies such as damages. If damages were considered to
be the just and appropriate remedy, the persons whose Charter rights have been
violated might have to proceed in a court of civil jurisdiction.A criminal trial court may not always be the
proper place to seek a s. 24(1) remedy. A person whose rights have been
violated may not be put on trial; the proceedings initiating the trial process
may not have yet been launched; the trial judge may have been involved in the
Charter violation: see R. v. Rahey (1987), 33 C.C.C. (3d) 289,
39 D.L.R. (4th) 481, [1987] 1 S.C.R. 588 (S.C.C.). The appropriate
and just remedy may be damages which a criminal trial court may not be deemed
to have power to award or, having such power, may not have monetary
jurisdiction to make an award in the amount warranted.

Assuming everything else in favour of the
accused, the question is whether the trial judge erred in law on the facts
found by him in granting such a remedy. In my view, he clearly did. He granted
the most sweeping and drastic remedy in the arsenal of remedies without any
factual basis that could possibly permit the conclusion that it would be either
just or appropriate to do so. He concluded as a fact that there was no malice
or negligence by either the Crown or the police. In the light of that
conclusion, the point as to whether the remedy could be granted is really not
arguable. The need to impress upon all parties the requirement that the law be
obeyed is not enough to justify granting a remedy which is not otherwise just
and appropriate. I say that with full recognition of the fundamental nature of
the right created by s. 454 and the importance of it being complied with by
those who are obligated to do so; but a breach does not in itself justify
turning the system on its head.The source of the error may be the view of
the trial judge, which is implicit in his decision, that having found that, in
connection with the charges before him there had been a breach of the rights of
the accused, he must grant some remedy. I will assume that for every breach of
a Charter right there is some remedy. It simply does not follow that every
breach must lead to some remedy being granted at trial. The purpose of the
trial is, as it was before the Charter, to decide whether the accused is
guilty. Breaches of Charter rights do not become a proper subject of inquiry at
trial simply because they occurred in relation to the charge being tried.

circumstances of the particular case.It is unnecessary to examine all of the

I am satisfied on the basis of the
authorities that I have set forth above that there is a residual discretion in
a trial court judge to stay proceedings where compelling an accused to stand
trial would violate those fundamental principles of justice which underlie the
community's sense of fair play and decency and to prevent the abuse of a
court's process through oppressive or vexatious proceedings. It is a power,
however, of special application which can only be exercised in the clearest of
cases.This statement was approved by the Supreme Court
of Canada in R. v. Jewitt (1985), 21 C.C.C. (3d) 7,
20 D.L.R. (4th) 651, [1985] 2 S.C.R. 128 (S.C.C.), and in R. v. Keyowski (1988),
40 C.C.C. (3d) 481, [1988] 1 S.C.R. 657, 62 C.R. (3d) 349 (S.C.C.).The Young case dealt with abuse of
process. It may be that the jurisprudence with regard to granting a stay with
respect to Charter breaches could be even more stringent than that sug­gested
by Dubin J. in Young because, in the case of Charter breaches, there is
usually a wider, range of remedies available and, moreover, the victim of the
breach has the further remedy of suing in civil court for what has become known
as a constitutional tort — a breach of a constitutional right.

The public has a vital interest in seeing that
persons who are accused of a crime are tried. A stay of proceedings should not
be allowed to interfere with the prosecution of an accused person to
conclusion. That may even be true of any s. 24(1) remedy except where the
breach in some way affects the trial itself.There are of course circumstances where a stay
is the only remedy. One of these, not necessarily concerned with a Charter
breach, is where there is an abuse of process to such a degree that a stay is
demanded: see Young, supra. Another circumstance is where it would be
unfair to allow the trial to proceed. That would generally involve a situation
where the accused person would be unable to make a full answer and defence.Another circumstance is where a stay is
warranted to prevent the continuation of an improper police practice. This
present case, or a fact situation corresponding with the present case, could be
illustrative of such a situation. In this particular case, the police practice
in respect of s. 503(1) had been relatively constant beforehand but the issue
that comes up in this case had, according to the evidence, not been raised
before. A stay may not be necessary in this case but, if it appeared that the
police were to revert to their former practice, the ordering of stays might be
the only way to end that practice.

A stay at trial may be appropriate where there
is a pattern of unreasonable delay in bringing matters on for trial which may
be attributed to the Crown.Stays should not be given as s. 24(1) remedies
except in special circumstances such as those illustrated above. The Charter is
not intended to defeat the criminal process but to protect citizens from
conduct that is contrary to those rights therein described. It is only when
interference with the criminal process is the only way in which the appropriate
remedy may be given — such as to prevent an unfair trial or to bring a stop to
improper practices — that a stay should be ordered.McIntyre J. in Mills, supra, expressed
the hope that trial judges would devise imaginative remedies but expressed the
reservationsthat such remedies should remain subject to
constitutional restraint. They must remain within the ambit of criminal powers.The powers of a trial judge in the Provincial
Court under s. 24(l) are relatively limited and almost appear in a case such as
this to require that the judge either stay the proceeding or leave the accused
to seek redress in a civil process in the Trial Division of the Supreme Court
of Newfoundland.Usually, the remedy that is sought where there
is a Charter breach is a stay of proceedings. If such is sought but not
justified in a particular case, the fact that an alternate remedy may not be
within the ambit of the powers of the trial court should be of no concern to
the trial judge. Such alternate remedy may be pursued elsewhere. It is true
that this makes it inconvenient for the person whose Charter rights have been
violated but inconvenience alone does not justify the granting of the extreme
remedy of a stay of proceedings.

There can be no doubt that the violation of the
respondent's s. 9 Charter right in this case was serious. The police had
several months in which to begin proceedings against her and for reasons
unknown to the court failed to do so. The matter was energized at the end of
February, 1993, but even then no action was taken that gave the impression that
the police had any sense of urgency whatsoever. Moreover, the police failed to
take any of the several alternative processes and in fact failed to lay any
charges until two days after she was arrested. Defence counsel had alerted the
police to the requirement of s. 501(3) during the detention.While the court does not receive the impression
that the police acted in bad faith, it seems that the police were totally
unaware of the civil rights of the respondent and seemed to have taken a rather
casual attitude towards her detention.However, the violation of her rights, while
serious, bears no relation to the charges laid against her. The respondent was
unlawfully imprisoned. This is a civil tort and a constitutional tort. The
respondent may seek her remedy in the Trial Division by another proceeding. The
charges against her should proceed because the trial would not be unfair and
there is no justification at this stage in ordering a stay for the purpose of
bringing to a halt improper administrative or judicial practices.

The appeal is allowed. The matter is remitted to
the Provincial Court for trial.GUSHUE J.A. concurs with GOODRIDGE
C.J.N.O'NEILL J.A. (dissenting):—This is an appeal from Kennedy Prov. Ct. J., who
entered a stay of proceedings, pursuant to s. 24(1) of the Canadian Charter
of Rights and Freedoms, prior to the scheduled trial of the respondent in
Provincial Court, in which court she had elected to be tried, and had pleaded
not guilty to charges of assault causing bodily harm, contrary to s. 267(l)(b)
of the Criminal Code and of public mischief, contrary to s. 140(l)(a) of
the Criminal Code.The incidents with respect to which the charges
were laid are alleged to have occurred on August 8, 1992. It appears that no
action was taken by the police until February 28, 1993, when Constable Crocker
of the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary became involved, although the public
mischief charge indicates that it arose out of an alleged false statement made
with intent to mislead an officer of the constabulary. Be that as it may, it
only came to the attention of Constable Crocker on that date and no real action
was taken by him with respect to questioning or apprehending the respondent
until Sunday, March 14, 1993, when he went to the respondent's residence in St.
John's and arrested her. There was evidence that the constable had previously
gone to the respondent's residence a couple of times, had knocked on the door,
but had gotten no response. There was also evidence that the constable had been
away from duty for 10 days during that period. Clearly, there seems to have
been no great urgency, at least on the constable's part, to take the respondent
into custody.

Following her arrest, which occurred at
approximately 1:30 p.m. on Sunday, the respondent was taken to a lock-up or
holding facility in St. John's and was not brought before a justice until late
in the morning of Tuesday, March 16, 1993, when she was released on conditions
that she avoid any contact with the complainant and members of the
complainant's family.The conditions attached to the respondent's release,
which were ones the constable had requested and to which the respondent
consented, were the very reasons why the respondent was held in custody, since
the constable wished to have these conditions made a prerequisite to the
respondent's release. The release, on conditions, could only be implemented by
a justice, or, as the constable believed, by a Provincial Court judge. The
respondent was not kept in custody for any other reason, such as being required
for questioning or to prevent the commission of any offence.The constable, in making the arrest was aware
that, as the system operated in St. John's, the respondent would remain in
custody until the first court day in Provincial Court following the arrest,
which, in this case, happened to be Tuesday because Monday was a provincial
holiday.While at the holding facility, the respondent
contacted a lawyer. The lawyer was told by the arresting officer that the
respondent would not be released since the police were not prepared to release
her without the conditions already referred to. When asked by counsel if the
respondent would be brought before a justice in accordance with s. 503(1) of
the Criminal Code, the police officer replied that she would not be
brought before a justice until Tuesday, March 16, 1993, when the Provincial
Court was sitting.

unconditionally, and so releases him.The section requires that a person such as the
respondent, arrested without warrant, which was the case here, and not released
under any other provision, be brought before a justice without unreasonable
delay, and, in any event, within a period of 24 hours following the arrest.

trans­portation, a justice, before whom an arrested person should be brought,

when he arrested the respondent on Sunday that she would not be brought before

Clearly, there was a breach of s. 503 of the Criminal
Code.Was there a breach of s. 9 of the Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms?We must now consider whether the detention of
the respondent was an arbitrary detention as contemplated by s. 9 of the
Charter:9. Everyone has the right not to be
arbitrarily detained or imprisoned.There was no system in place in St. John's
whereby the obligation placed on a peace officer by s. 503 of the Criminal
Code could be observed. However, in the rural parts of this province, which
for the most part are policed by the R.C.M.P., a procedure is in place whereby
justices are available to permit the police officers serving in these areas to
comply with s. 503. What is even more surprising is that the constabulary,
which also polices the City of Corner Brook, had implemented a policy of having
justices availa­ble as required under s. 503. .In the situation here, while it cannot be said
that there was a deliberate effort on the part of the police constable not to
comply with the provisions of s. 503(1), no effort was made to comply with the
section either by the police officer, by those in authority in the
constabulary, or by those involved in the administration of justice and in a
position to institute and implement a system whereby the section could be
complied with. Neither the arresting officer nor his superior officers who were
called as witnesses seemed aware of the obligation of a peace officer to comply
with s. 503. Even if one could argue that the 24-hour period referred to in s.
503(1)(b) were the applicable period, and not "without unreasonable
delay", as is the real obligation, there was not even any effort to comply
with that.

This was not a question whether there was a
failure to comply with the system for some technical reasons or an oversight —
a falling through the cracks. The respondent's detention occurred because of
what could be termed a deliberate policy on the part of those charged with the
responsibility for the administration of justice to ignore the very clear
direction embodied in s. 503. However, whether it occurred by neglect or
deliberate policy, where there was a failure to provide a system whereby
justices are made available, and a detention occurs because of that failure,
then that detention is arbitrary within the meaning of s. 9 of the Charter.In the factum of the appellant, there is a
footnote indicating that: "a system of having Provincial Court judges
available to conduct judicial interim release hearings on weekends is now in
place".The remedy under s. 24(1)Section 24 of the Charter is as follows:24(1) Anyone whose rights or freedoms, as
guaranteed by this Charter, have been infringed or denied may apply to a court
of competent jurisdiction to obtain such remedy as the court considers
appropriate and just in the circumstances.(2) Where, in proceedings under subsection
(1), a court concludes that evidence was obtained in a manner that infringed or
denied any rights or freedoms guaranteed by this Charter, the evidence shall be
excluded if it is established that, having regard to all the circumstances, the
admission of it in the proceedings would bring the administration of justice
into disrepute.

In his argument, Crown counsel argued that the
trial judge did not sufficiently inquire into alternative remedies available
under s. 24(1) of the Charter such as a reduction in sentence or an award of
damages. He also argued that the remedy of habeas corpus was open to the
respondent.The trial judge considered the remedy of a
reduction in sentence and concluded, in my view, correctly, that such was not
an appropriate remedy. His reasons for so concluding are set out later in this
decision; I agree with his reasons and conclusion.With respect to an award of damages, I have very
grave doubts as to whether a Provincial Court judge, sitting on what might be
called the criminal side, would have jurisdiction to make an award of damages.
There is also the problem that whereas the Provincial Court, on its civil side,
has jurisdiction to award damages, the amount which may be awarded in that
court is limited. Assuming then that a Provincial Court judge were to have that
jurisdiction, (and I make no decision as to his right to do so in a criminal
matter), and were to conclude that the appropriate damages to be awarded as a
remedy were in excess of the civil jurisdiction of the Provincial Court, the
applicant would then have to make an application in the Supreme Court where the
matter would presum­ably be argued with the attendant increased legal fees,
delay and inconvenience.

corpus was that counsel for the respondent, having been advised that the
respondent would not be brought before a justice before Tuesday morning, could
have sought her release through habeas corpus or by a s. 24(1)
application in the Supreme Court of Newfoundland. For very obvious reasons,
neither of these steps was a reasonable alternative. Nothing further need be
said with respect to these submissions.In R. v. Sullivan (1991), unreported
[reported 96 Nfld. & P.E.I.R. 7, 13 W.C.B. (2d) 547], this court
dealt with an application for a remedy for a breach of s. 9 of the Charter
where an accused person had been detained for some 28 hours following his
arrest. Gushue J.A., having stated that the court was prepared to accept, for
the purposes of the case, that the accused had been arbitrarily imprisoned,
went on to state [at p. 9]:[The accused] had been charged with three
serious offences and, unquestiona­bly, had he appeared before the court within
the statutory period, he would have been remanded in custody pending a bail
application, as he indeed was when he did appear. While his rights had been
breached and he was entitled to apply for a remedy under s. 24(1) of the
Charter, it is clear that the breach was not of a serious nature.

The staying of criminal charges against an
accused person is obviously the ultimate response by the courts to
infringements of that person's constitu­tional rights or an abuse of court process
and should only be utilized in the most serious and clearest cases. While a
judge is given the discretion under s. 24(1) to grant a remedy which "the
court considers just and appropriate in the circumstances", it does not
follow that the court is thereby given an unqualified right to deal with a
breach as it sees fit. Any remedy granted must be for good reason in the
circumstances of the particular case.Clearly, Sullivan can be distinguished
from the matter before us. The respondent here was just 21 years of age at the
time of her arrest, she was a resident of St. John's, there was no evidence of
any criminal record, and the alleged incidents giving rise to the charge had
occurred some seven or eight months prior to her arrest. Further, the respondent
had denied to the arresting officer her involvement with respect to at least
one of the charges and the police officer had indicated that he had no reason
to keep her for more than an hour or so and that he was prepared to have her
released provided that she entered into the conditions already referred to.Although considerable evidence was adduced at
the hearing with respect to the practices of the Royal Newfoundland
Constabulary and the R.C.M.P. with respect to the availability or
non-availability of Provincial Court judges, and the availability and ability
of justices to deal with the release of persons arrested, no evidence
whatsoever was introduced or sought to be introduced with respect to the
seriousness of the matters or incidents giving rise to the charges brought
against the respondent, or as to why she was arrested on a Sunday during a long
weekend, as opposed to being served with a summons to appear following the
laying of an information. I might add that the actual information setting forth
the charges against the respondent was not actually sworn to until March 14th,
just shortly before the release of the respondent.

In his decision the trial judge said at p. 87:While the court has found that there was no
police policy to detain all persons arrested outside the periods of time when
the Provincial Court in St. John's is sitting, the court did find that this was
the practice. Further the court found that the practice operates in all but
exceptional cases.The practice operates to deprive individuals
who have been detained of their liberty in an arbitrary manner. Everyone
familiar with the justice system in St. John's is aware of the practice. It
does operate in a manner wherein people are arbitrarily
detained. To equate the availability of a justice under s. 503(1) of the Code to the hours when court is in
session is not an acceptable practice.In considering the remedies which may be
available to a court on such an application, the trial judge reviewed cases
where courts had afforded, as a remedy, a substantial reduction in the penalty
which might otherwise have been imposed. He went on to state that in his
opinion, that particular remedy would not be appropri­ate in the manner before
him. He said:First, the application has been brought
pre-trial. The accused is of course at this stage presumed innocent. The remedy
would have to be held in abeyance until the end of the trial and applied only
if the accused were found guilty. It is a remedy that can only be applied after
a trial and a conviction and is not a remedy which could apply in the event of
an acquittal. It is therefore only a potential remedy contingent upon a
conviction and cannot be applied in event of an acquittal. It would be no
remedy if that result were attained.

And later:A reduced sentence, even a substantially
reduced one, would not adequately address the deprivation of liberty involved.
The deprivation of liberty in an arbitrary manner is a serious violation of the
Charter. The deprivation of liberty commenced with the refusal of the police to
act under s. 503 of the Code. After having been asked by duty counsel if
they would arrange for the appearance of the accused before a justice, they
failed to act. The officer simply indicated that the accused would be held
until Court was open on Tuesday morning. The failure to act when asked to do so
made the violation of the right all the more serious and flagrant.In arriving at his conclusion to enter a stay of
proceedings, the trial judge stated:There is no doubt that the offences before
the court are serious ones. In the situation when the court confronts serious
charges and a serious rights violation it must consider what remedy is
appropriate. I have delineated each of the remedies and offered my opinion on
the appropriateness of them in regard
to the circumstances of this case.The failure to act in accordance with the Criminal
Code provisions relating to bringing the accused before a justice resulted
in a substantial deprivation of liberty in an arbitrary manner. The liberty of
individuals is a cherished societal value. An arbitrary deprivation of liberty
is not acceptable to society. To afford no remedy at all would be to condone
the deprivation of liberty.

serious charges a remedy must be granted. So serious and flagrant was the
violation, I feel that it is not appropriate to permit the charges to proceed —
all other remedies are inadequate.He concluded:I feel that no remedy short of a stay of
proceedings would address in an appropriate and just manner the arbitrary
detention in the circumstances of this case.The matter of the appropriateness of the remedy
here is one vested in the Provincial Court judge, sitting as a court of
competent jurisdiction. The trial judge in exercising the discretion granted to
him by s. 24(l) of the Charter, thoroughly canvassed the various remedies which
might be applicable and concluded that no remedy short of a stay of proceedings
would be appropriate and just.I cannot say that in the circumstances of this
case the trial judge was in error in exercising his discretion under s. 24(1)
of the Charter by entering a stay of proceedings.I would dismiss the appeal.Appeal allowed.[ScanLII Collection]

Corporation arguing Guardian's office of Church directing criminal acts was autonomous
-- Trial judge properly instructing jury issue was whether those with de facto
control of corporation authorized or carried out criminal acts -- Appeal
dismissed. Criminal law -- Sentence -- Breach of trust -- Church of Scientology
arranging for Church members to obtain employment with government agencies
identified by Church as enemies -- Members taking documents and providing them
to Church in breach of their oaths of office -- Church fined $250,000 and
person who directed operation fined $5,000 -- Sentence affirmed on appeal. The appellants were charged with breach of trust and theft. In the 1970s,
the Guardian's Office of the appellant Church of Scientology allegedly
authorized Church members to infiltrate government agencies which the Church
viewed as enemies. Included as targets were the Ontario Provincial Police
(OPP), and the Ministry of the Attorney General of Ontario. Those members
obtained employment with the agencies and, in breach of their oaths of office,
took copies of confidential documents and provided them to the Church. The
appellant M was responsible for supervising the agents who had been planted in
the various government agencies and other organizations. While executing a search warrant at the offices of the Church, the police
ignored a limitation in the search warrant which directed them to seize only
documents in the described categories or classes if they related to certain
specified time periods and related directly to the described offences. The
police seized approximately two million documents. They seized documents if
they fell within the class of documents and the time period irrespective of
whether the documents related directly to the described offences. The trial
judge ruled that the seizure went far beyond what was authorized by the search
warrant and that the manner in which the search was conducted tainted the
entire seizure and violated the appellants' rights under s. 8 of the Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms. He ruled that the seized evidence should be excluded
under s. 24(2) of the Charter. The defence also sought exclusion of
"secondary evidence" in the form of the testimony of five Crown
witnesses who were discovered as a result of the seized documents. The trial
judge held that there was a causal connection, if not a temporal connection,
between the Charter violation and the evidence obtained from the witnesses and
that the evidence had accordingly been obtained in a manner that infringed the
appellants' Charter rights. He concluded that the exclusion of the secondary
evidence in connection with the less serious offences of theft would not bring
the administration of justice into disrepute, but that to exclude the secondary
evidence on the more serious charges of breach of trust would bring the administration
of justice into disrepute. The evidence was admitted on the breach of trust
counts.

The appellants argued at trial that the exclusion of certain groups from the
jury roll, in particular non-citizens, violated their rights under ss. 7, 11
and 15 of the Charter. That challenge was rejected. It was the position of the Church at trial that it was not legally
responsible for the actions of "renegade members" in the Guardian's
Office. The Crown relied on the identification doctrine of criminal responsibility,
which holds a corporation liable for the criminal acts of its board of
directors and of employees who are the corporation's "alter ego" or
"directing mind", where those acts are performed within the scope of
the person's authority, where the directing mind was not acting totally in
fraud of the corporation and where the act was intended to and does result in
benefit exclusively to the directing mind. The appellants were convicted on two counts of breach of trust. The Church
was fined $250,000 and M was fined $5,000. The Church and M both appealed the
conviction and the Church also appealed the sentence. In addition to the
Charter issues identified above, they argued that the identification doctrine
of corporate criminal liability does not apply to a non-profit corporation
without share capital established for religious purposes such as the Church and
that the application of the identification doctrine to the Church violated ss.
2(a), (d), 7 and 11(d) of the Charter. They also attacked the adequacy of Crown
disclosure, arguing that the trial judge erred in ruling that the Crown was not
required to provide the defence with an inventory of all the material in the
possession of the OPP that had not been disclosed to the defence.

input:
Held, the appeal should be dismissed. In view of the extensive disclosure that had been made by the Crown, the
further demand for the OPP inventory was speculative, fanciful, disruptive,
unmeritorious, obstructive and time-consuming. Despite the mass of material
that was disclosed to the defence over the many hearings leading up to the
trial and the trial itself, defence counsel at trial and on the appeal were
unable to point to a single document that might exist that would be relevant to
the case and that had not been disclosed. It was open to the trial judge to find that the strength of the causal
connection between the breach of s. 8 of the Charter and the obtaining of the
secondary evidence was such that the evidence was procured in a manner that
infringed the appellants' Charter rights. It was conceded that the admission of
the secondary evidence would not affect the fairness of the trial. The
secondary evidence did not have the quality of self- incrimination and did not
emanate from the appellants. The mere use by the authorities of documents
created by the appellants before the violation to obtain further evidence was
not the kind of compelled participation that would render this after-acquired
evidence "conscriptive evidence" so as to affect the fairness of the
trial. While the violation of the appellants' s. 8 rights was serious, the conduct
of the police in ignoring the limiting provisions of the warrant had to be
balanced against the consequences to the appellant of a more detailed review on
the premises. The fact that the police were acting upon a valid search warrant
was also a proper factor to take into account.

The breach of trust offences, unlike the theft offences, were serious. The
fact that the efforts of the appellant to obtain confidential information were
largely unsuccessful did not mitigate the serious nature of the offences. The
distinction the trial judge drew between the breach of trust counts and the
theft counts, and his conclusion that the admission of the evidence would bring
the administration of justice into disrepute with respect to the latter counts
but not with respect to the former counts, were reasonable. The appellants did not have standing to assert a violation of the equality
rights of non-citizens who are excluded from the jury pool. While an accused
may defend a criminal charge by arguing that the law under which he or she is
charged is unconstitutional, that was not the defence raised here. The
appellants were required to show that the manner in which the jury panel was
selected infringed their rights as accused persons. Their rights as accused
flowed primarily from ss. 11(d) and (f) of the Charter. The Church could not rely on s. 7 of the Charter in support of its argument
with respect to jury selection, as a corporation cannot invoke s. 7. While M
could invoke s. 7, the fundamental justice guarantee in s. 7 added nothing to
her claim. The claim based on s. 7 was an attempt, indirectly, to acquire
standing to argue the equality rights of potential jurors. Even if s. 7
incorporates the equality rights under s. 15, it only incorporates the equality
rights of the person whose liberty is at stake. The liberty of non-citizens who
may be affected by the alleged discriminatory nature of the Juries Act, R.S.O.
1990, c. J.3, was not at stake in this prosecution.

The right to a representative jury roll is not absolute in the sense that
the accused is entitled to a roll representative of all of the many groups that
make up Canadian society. There is no characteristic that persons bring to the
fact-finding process of the jury based solely on their immigration status.
Canadian citizens are of all races, nationalities, ethnic origin, colour,
religion, sex, age and ability. Immigration status is not a relevant
characteristic when regard is had to the rationale underlying the right to a
representative pool. The appellants' rights under s. 11(d) and 11(f) of the
Charter were not violated. The identification doctrine applies to non-profit corporations established
for religious purposes, such as the appellant Church. The Church could not argue that its prosecution through the identification
doctrine violated s. 7 of the Charter as s. 7 does not apply to corporations.
The Church's inability to rely on s. 7 also foreclosed any argument based on an
alleged infringement of s. 11(d) of the Charter. The presumption of innocence
in s. 11(d) requires that before an accused can be convicted, the trier of fact
must be satisfied beyond a reasonable doubt of the existence of all of the
essential elements of the offence. These essential elements include not only
those set out in the relevant statute, but also those required as a matter of
fundamental justice by s. 7 of the Charter. The identification doctrine imposes
liability upon the corporation for the unlawful acts of its directing minds,
whether or not the board of directors authorized or was even aware of the acts,
and whether or not the board exercised due diligence to prevent the commission
of those acts. Since s. 7 of the Charter does not apply to corporate liability,
no additional elements are implied. The Church's rights under s. 11(d) were
therefore not infringed.

Assuming, without deciding, that the identification doctrine constitutes a
non-trivial burden on the practice of the Scientology religion and therefore
infringes s. 2(a) of the Charter, the infringement was justified under s. 1 of
the Charter. It was necessary to resort to a s. 1 analysis because one cannot
reformulate the common law doctrine of corporate criminal liability in a way
that would not infringe s. 2(a). The mere prosecution of the Church would
stigmatize the parishioners and members and divert funds from religious
purposes to defence of the charges. Even if the prosecution were limited to the
acts of the board of directors, it would infringe freedom of religion since
liability would still be imposed on the corporation on a vicarious basis. The
"innocent" parishioners would be required to fund the defence, and
Church property would be at risk if the Church were convicted and a fine
imposed. The objective of applying the identifiction doctrine to corporations
with religious objects is that no person is above or beyond the law. Having regard to the important position that corporations occupy in modern
society, subjecting corporations, including those with religious objects, to
the ordinary criminal law is a pressing and substantial objective and is
implied by the rule of law. The identification doctrine is a pragmatic, but rational, way of making a
corporation liable for criminal acts committed on its behalf or at least partly
for its benefit. It imposes liability only for the acts of the corporate
governing body and those to whom that body has delegated executive authority.
Moreover, even if the employee is deemed to be a directing mind of the
corporation, the corporation will not be liable for that employee's acts if
they are in total fraud of the corporation. Given these limitations on the
identification doctrine, it is rationally connected to the objective.

The application of the identification doctrine to non-profit religious
corporations infringes freedom of religion as little as possible. The appellant
suggested the imposition of corporate criminal liability, in the case of a
non-profit religious corporation, only where the board of directors either
authorized the illegal activity or failed to exercise due diligence to prevent
it. However, failing to impose corporate criminal liability for the acts of the
directing minds who are not on the board of directors fails to take into
account one of the fundamental rationales for imposing criminal liability on
the corporation in the first place. The wrongdoing of the agents of a
corporation is not done in a vacuum and, ordinarily, not solely to profit the
individual agent. The agents often commit the criminal acts to protect the
institution and its reputation. To fail to impose criminal liability on the
corporation for acts of persons with managerial responsibility acting in the
name of the corporation would result in a substantial gap in the deterrent
objective of the criminal law. Moreover, it was unclear how the appellant's
proposed alternative would impair freedom of religion any less than the
identification doctrine. Further, if the courts were to adopt a lower standard
of criminal liability for corporations with religious objects, this would
necessarily invite inquiry into whether these objects were genuine or a mere
sham to take advantage of the preferential treatment. Given the limits on the reach of the identification doctrine and the
importance of the rule of law and protection of the vulnerable, there is an
appropriate proportionality between the deleterious effects of the application
of the identification doctrine and the objective. The deleterious effects do
not outweigh the salutary effects, and it is a reasonable limit pursuant to s.
1 of the Charter.

The Church argued that the trial judge erred in not instructing the jury
that to find it guilty on the basis of the identification doctrine, it had to
be shown that persons alleged to be the directing minds of the corporation had
been delegated authority to design and supervise the implementation of corporate
policy. However, the Church operated in the context of a rigid command
structure in which the board of directors was irrelevant. The board of
directors did not appoint, much less delegate, senior officals of the Church.
At trial, the issues of corporate liability did not concern whether the illegal
acts were carried out with the knowledge of or by persons with executive
authority. The only real issues were whether information-gathering was within
the scope of authority of the persons in control of the Guardian's Office and,
more importantly, whether the Guardian's Office was an autonomous body,
separate and apart from the Toronto Church. The trial judge's instructions on
these two issues were clear and unimpeachable. It was obvious that the jury was
satisfied that information-gathering was a field of operation of the Toronto
Church and that the persons in the Guardian's Office performing those
operations were not part of an autonomous body, separate and apart from the
delivery of Church services. Once the jury found that the Guardian's Office was
not an autonomous body, they were bound to find the Church liable for the
unlawful acts committed by the persons in that office, inasmuch as de facto
control resided there.

appellants' acts constituted a deliberate attempt to undermine the
effectiveness of the O.P.P. and the Ministry of the Attorney General and struck

intended consequences of the offences. It was not a mitigating factor that the

the Church or anything that impaired the functioning of the agencies. Remorse

output:
The fines imposed on the appellants represented a fit sentence. The
appellants' acts constituted a deliberate attempt to undermine the
effectiveness of the O.P.P. and the Ministry of the Attorney General and struck
at the integrity of the public service. The trial judge properly focused on the
intended consequences of the offences. It was not a mitigating factor that the
persons planted in the agencies were unable to obtain anything of real value to
the Church or anything that impaired the functioning of the agencies. Remorse
was also not a mitigating factor in this case. The Church at no time admitted
responsibility for the offences or expressed remorse for its involvement. The
trial judge did not err in considering general deterrence to be the principal
objective in determining the amount of the fine. APPEAL from a conviction on two counts of breach of trust and from sentence.<decision><title>Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. R.</title>, <citation>[1985] 1 S.C.R. 662</citation>,

The judgment of the court was delivered by ROSENBERG J.A.: -- I. INTRODUCTION A. Overview of the case On June 25, 1992, the Church of Scientology of Toronto and Jacqueline Matz
were each convicted of two counts of breach of trust contrary to s. 111 of the
Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1970, c. C-34 (now R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, s. 122)
following a trial before Southey J. and a jury. The Church of Scientology of
Toronto was fined $250,000 and Jacqueline Matz was fined $5,000. The Church of
Scientology of Toronto appeals both the convictions and the sentence. Jacqueline
Matz appeals the conviction only. The charges arose from activities conducted by the intelligence bureau
within the Guardian's Office, a management arm of the appellant, Church of
Scientology of Toronto. Between 1974 and 1976, Scientologists secured employment
with government agencies perceived to be enemies of the church, and signed
oaths of secrecy as public officials. In breach of their oaths of office, they
then took copies of confidential documents from the agencies that employed them
and provided them to the Church of Scientology of Toronto. The appellant,
Jacqueline Matz, was a "case officer" and "Director of
Operations", and was responsible for supervising the agents who had been
planted in the various government agencies and other organizations.

B. Verdict at trial The indictment originally included 12 counts, consisting of seven counts of
theft and five counts of breach of trust. The theft counts related to theft of
documents from government agencies and other organizations. The breach of trust
counts related only to government agencies. As a result of a pre-trial ruling
excluding certain evidence under s. 24(2) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms, the Crown was left with no admissible evidence on the theft counts.
These charges were severed from the indictment, and acquittals were entered.
The jury convicted the appellants of breach of trust in relation to the Ontario
Provincial Police and the Ministry of the Attorney General of Ontario. The
appellants were acquitted on a second count involving the Ontario Provincial
Police and on charges relating to the Metropolitan Toronto Police and the Royal
Canadian Mounted Police. C. Theories of the parties This was a long and complex trial in which virtually everything was in
issue. Many of the same issues now form grounds of appeal. In summary, it was
the position of the Crown that the appellant Church of Scientology of Toronto,
a non- profit religious corporation, had authorized members of the church to
infiltrate government agencies and other organizations such as the Canadian
Mental Health Association in order to obtain information that would be of use
to the church. It was the Crown's theory that the appellant perceived that it
was under attack by these organizations. The appellant resorted to the
"plant" operations when other more direct means, such as break and
enter, were judged to be too dangerous. These operations were run by Jacqueline
Metz out of the intelligence bureau, which was an arm of the Guardian's Office
within the church. The Crown relied on the doctrine of corporate criminal
liability as explained in Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. R., [1985] 1 S.C.R.
662, 19 C.C.C. (3d) 1, which, subject to certain conditions, holds a
corporation liable for the acts of certain of its agents.

It was the position of the appellant, the Church of Scientology of Toronto,
that it was not legally responsible for the actions of its "renegade
members" in the Guardian's Office who had failed to follow church
doctrine. The appellant contended that the information-gathering functions
carried out by the Guardian's office in Toronto were assigned to it by the
Church of Scientology of California (U.K.) (Guardian Office World Wide), not by
the Church of Scientology of Toronto. The appellant also made the broad submission
that the doctrine of corporate criminal liability does not apply to non-profit
religious corporations. The appellant Matz did not testify. The theory of her defence was based on
gaps in the Crown's case with respect to each of the counts. In relation to the
charge involving the O.P.P., she argued that there was no breach of trust since
the information obtained by the agent was unimportant. With respect to the
count involving the Ministry of the Attorney General, she argued that the
Crown's evidence was unreliable and that, in one of the incidents relied on by
the Crown, no confidential information seems to have been obtained. D. Corporate management structure A critical aspect of this appeal concerns the application of the doctrine of
corporate criminal liability to a non-profit religious corporation. The
application of the doctrine is complicated by the unconventional corporate
structure adopted by the various corporate members of the Church of
Scientology, including the Church of Scientology of Toronto.

input:
At the time material to this case, the Church of Scientology was a
world-wide organization with a hierarchical structure. L. Ron Hubbard, the
Founder, stood at the top of the hierarchy in England. Second in command was
Mary Sue Hubbard, the Controller. Directly beneath her was Jane Kember, the
Guardian. Below these officials, Scientology organizations were separately
incorporated in various cities throughout the world. The Church of Scientology
of Toronto was one such organization. The Church of Scientology of Toronto was incorporated as a corporation
without share capital on September 8, 1967 under the Ontario Corporations Act,
R.S.O. 1960, c. 71 (now R.S.O. 1990, c. C.38). The administration of the
corporation and, indeed, of all Scientology organizations, was dictated by a
series of policies written by the Founder, L. Ron Hubbard. These policies
governed a variety of administrative matters, including the command and
communication channels, the positions within the organization and the division
of responsibilities among Scientology officials. The Church of Scientology of Toronto was managed through two command
structures. The FLAG bureau, which was part of the Sea Organization, was
responsible for the day-to-day delivery of Scientology services to the public
at the local Toronto organization ("Org"). The Org was under the
management and control of an executive director. The executive director
received direction from his seniors in the FLAG Bureau network, who received
direction from L. Ron Hubbard.

input:
The other management structure was the Guardian's Office. Its purpose was to
help L. Ron Hubbard enforce and issue policy to safeguard Scientology
organizations. Like the FLAG bureau, the Guardian's Office was run along
hierarchical reporting lines. The Guardian's Office Toronto reported to the
Guardian's Office Canada, which in turn reported to the Guardian's Office World
Wide, and ultimately to L. Ron Hubbard. Directions were sent
"down-lines" through the same structure. Like the Guardian's Office World Wide and the Guardian's Office Canada, the
Guardian's Office Toronto was comprised of four bureaus, each of which was
delegated a specific sphere of managerial authority. These bureaus were: the
legal bureau, the finance bureau, the public relations bureau and the
intelligence bureau. The purpose of the intelligence bureau was to find out
about those whom L. Ron Hubbard had identified as Scientology's enemies so that
attacks could be diverted before they became public issues. When he established
the Guardian's Office, L. Ron Hubbard issued a policy letter entitled "The
Guardian", which assigned intelligence functions to that office, and
described the purpose of intelligence in colourful terms: By such studies one can predict which way cats
are going to jump and organize to meet situations which may threaten
Scientology from possible enemies or to take advantage of situations which
might benefit Scientology. The intelligence bureau of the Guardian's Office Toronto carried out the
plant operations that were the subject-matter of the charges.

On the theory of the Crown, while the two management structures, the FLAG
bureau and the Guardian's Office, had different functions, both were integral
to the operation of the Church of Scientology of Toronto. Although the local
Guardian's Office took direction from, and reported to, its senior officials in
England, it exercised a senior management function within the local church. The
management of the local Org could not tell the Guardian's Office what to do; in
contrast, the Guardian's Office could, and did, give orders to local management
regarding the safety and security of Scientology. The operations of The
Guardian's Office Toronto were financed by money collected by the local Org. On the theory of the appellant church, the Guardian's Office was separate
from the Church of Scientology of Toronto. It was autonomous and self-ruling
and not fixed to any local Church of Scientology. It had its own doctrine and
policy. In particular, the appellant argued that the intelligence operations

in England. While there, he confirmed that the intelligence-gathering
techniques could include "rip-offs", that is, the placing of agents
and the theft of files. The Guardian World Wide, Jane Kember, identified
targets. She was particularly interested in the O.P.P., the Ministry of the
Attorney General and the Metropolitan Toronto Police. She made it Mr. Levman's
mandate to obtain files from these organizations. After returning to Canada in
the fall of 1973, Mr. Levman took steps to implement the guardian's
instructions. He evaluated candidates to be planted in the "enemy"
organizations. The plant operations were under the purview of the intelligence
bureau of the Guardian's Office Toronto. Mr. Levman and Ms. Evoy both received
reports on the activities of the plants. An important event leading to the use of plants rather than more direct
illegal means was the arrest of Alan Coulson and Michael Chornopesky in April
1974. They were arrested while attempting to break into a law firm that was
acting for former members of Scientology who were engaged in litigation with
the church. Levman had ordered this break-in as he was to be a witness on an

him. Mr. Levman and others took elaborate precautions to erase any connection
between Coulson and Chornopesky and Scientology. After this incident, Jane
Kember instructed Levman and Evoy not to conduct break and enters. Instead,

they were investigating Scientology. Cynthia Bake became a plant at the O.P.P.
after being approached by a case worker for the Guardian's Office intelligence
bureau. Ms. Bake was a "public person" in the Church of Scientology
of Toronto; she was not a staff member, but taking courses at the Toronto
location. She obtained a clerk position with the O.P.P. intelligence branch in
the general headquarters building. She swore an oath of office and secrecy, and
worked in this capacity from May 1976 until November 1976. As a plant, Ms. Bake reported to Jacqueline Matz. She testified at trial
that she was pressured by Ms. Matz to find out what was in the O.P.P. files.
She looked in the files, but could not find anything relating to Scientology.
She took another piece of paper, which referred to the "Moonies", and
gave it to Ms. Matz. Eventually, Ms. Bake did not wish to continue acting as a
plant, and she resigned.

inside and the two of them looked for files relating to the Church of
Scientology. Ms. Evoy testified that they searched in the office of Donald

Before discussing these main grounds of appeal, I turn to several grounds of
appeal that can be disposed of with brief reasons. II. ORDER OF CLOSING ADDRESSES In her factum, the appellant Matz argues that the provisions of s. 651 of
the Criminal Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. C-46, that dictate the order of closing
addresses violate her rights under ss. 7 and 11 of the Charter. In view of the
decision of this court in R. v. Rose (1996), 28 O.R. (3d) 602, 35 C.R.R. (2d)
229, leave to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada granted February 7, 1997
(subsequent to the hearing of this appeal), no oral submissions were made on
this point. This ground of appeal fails. III. SIMILAR FACT EVIDENCE The appellants submit that the trial judge erred in permitting the Crown to
introduce evidence of criminal acts, other than those in the indictment,
allegedly committed by members of the Church of Scientology of Toronto. For
example, he permitted the Crown to lead evidence that staff from the Guardian's
Office had broken into government offices and other organizations. Evidence was
led about the arrest of the two Scientology members, Coulson and Chornopesky,
who had attempted to break into a law firm that was acting for former members
of Scientology engaged in litigation with the church. Evidence was also led of
an attempt to obtain a file from the Ministry of the Attorney General by
impersonation of one of the ministry's counsel.

In our view, the trial judge did not err by admitting this "similar act
evidence". He initially held that this evidence was admissible as tending
to show that the acts charged were committed with the knowledge and authority
of the Church of Scientology of Toronto. The evidence was relevant to the issue
of whether the Guardian's Office was acting on behalf of the corporate
appellant. As this court noted in Canadian Dredge & Dock Co. v. R., (1981),
56 C.C.C. (2d) 193 at p. 293, "Proof of the repetition of wrongful acts by
the agents of a corporation may be sufficient to permit a jury to infer that
the acts charged in the indictment were carried out with the knowledge and
approval of those in charge of the corporation". Some of the evidence,
especially that relating to the arrest of Coulson and Chornopesky, was also
admissible as part of the narrative to explain steps taken by the Guardian's
Office in relation to the charged acts. By the end of the case, the trial judge had concluded that this evidence was
not relevant to any issue in dispute and he instructed the jury accordingly.
For example, the trial judge directed the jury as follows: The Crown has led evidence of other criminal acts
alleged to have been done by Scientologists. I have not referred to this
evidence, because, if believed, it goes no further than to show that the
criminal acts were committed with the authority of the Guardian Office in
Toronto, and it was for that purpose that I permitted this similar fact
evidence to be given. But that evidence throws no light one way or the other on
the point in issue as to whether the persons in the Guardian Office in Toronto
were acting within the field of operation of Church of Scientology of Toronto
that had been assigned to them.

Now, there is a very important point that I asked
you to keep in mind respecting this evidence of other criminal acts. You must
not rely on this evidence as evidence that Church of Scientology of Toronto had
a propensity to condone or authorize criminal offences, and so was likely to
have authorized the criminal acts with which it is here charged. You should not
rely on this evidence of other criminal acts in any way in determining the
guilt or innocence of the individuals accused in any of the counts before you.
It can only be used by you for the limited purpose I have explained in
determining the guilt or innocence of the corporate accused, the Church of
Scientology of Toronto. And I repeat, in my view it does not advance the case
there, because it only takes you to the Guardian Office, and then you are faced
with the question: "Was the Guardian Office the directing mind
of Church of Scientology of Toronto in a field of operation assigned to it? And
was it not totally in fraud of that corporation? And was it, by design or
result, for the benefit of that corporation?" (Emphasis added) Similar forceful directions to ignore this evidence on the issue of
corporate criminal liability were repeated on several occasions. The appellants were not unfairly prejudiced by the admission of this
evidence. In fact, the trial judge's instruction to the jury to ignore this
evidence was overly favourable to the appellants. This ground of appeal fails.

opinion on the central issues in the case, and usually in a manner favouring

In 1981, while Marion Evoy was the Deputy Guardian Canada, she was
investigated by members of the Sea Organization and required to enter into a
program of confession and punishment because of her involvement in illegal
acts. She was told to write out a list of her actions and to admit, in writing,
that she was responsible for all of the actions she had directed. Ms. Evoy
gradually withdrew from the church and, in the fall of 1984, entered into an
immunity agreement similar to that of Ms. Fairfield. Mr. Norris argues that the trial judge did not give an adequate warning as
to the danger of relying on the evidence of the Crown witnesses, as required by
R. v. Vetrovec, [1982] 1 S.C.R. 811, 67 C.C.C. (2d) 1. Mr. Norris also argues
that the evidence relied on by the Crown to confirm the testimony of the Crown
witnesses did not in fact do so. We only called upon Crown counsel to respond
to the latter argument. A. Adequacy of the Vetrovec warning In Vetrovec, Dickson J. held that where the trial judge decides that some
caution should be given to the jury about the evidence of suspect witnesses, no
particular rule, formula or direction must be followed. He held at p. 831
S.C.R. that what may be appropriate is a "clear and sharp warning to attract
the attention of the juror to the risks of adopting, without more, the evidence
of the witness".
